title: Chinese AI Firms Rush to Reserve Overseas Nvidia Capacity Amid Curbs Fear
excerpt: Reuters, citing three people familiar with the matter, reported Chinese AI companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered capacity overseas over fears Washington will regulate remote access to restricted processors.
body:
• Chinese AI companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centres outside China, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
  • The concern, as reported, is that the scandal involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could add momentum to the Remote Access Security Act, which would let the US Commerce Department regulate remote access to restricted technology.
  • That bill passed the US House 369-22 in January and awaits Senate action, according to Reuters — it is not yet law.
  • For readers in tech: no volumes, prices or signed contracts for the capacity sought were reported, so this is a reported rush to reserve, not confirmed new supply.

Chinese artificial intelligence companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centres outside China, Reuters reported on November 12, 2026, citing three people familiar with the matter. The companies are worried, Reuters said, that the scandal involving the US chipmaker's chief executive, Jensen Huang, could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their remote use of advanced processors. Unite.AI set out what the pending bill would do, citing Reuters and the Congress tracker.

Access without importing the chips

Washington restricts exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips, Reuters reported, but Chinese companies can access them remotely by renting computing power overseas. That distinction — shipping a processor versus renting its computing service — is the gap at issue. Restricting overseas cloud access would make high-end computing harder for Chinese developers to obtain without importing chips directly.

Reuters said a major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally whether to lock in overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some companies have contacted data-centre operators about reserving it. The people declined to be identified, or to identify the cloud provider, because of the sensitivity of the matter. Smaller AI labs are considering similar steps, including approaching major providers of rented computing power in Southeast Asia, two of the people said.

The bill the companies fear

The companies fear the controversy surrounding Huang could add political momentum to the Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, Reuters reported. The bill would give the Commerce Department authority to regulate remote, cloud-based access to restricted technology. The House of Representatives passed the bill in January by a 369-22 vote, and it awaits Senate action.

Unite.AI, citing the Congress tracker, added that the Senate received the bill on January 13, 2026, and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and that the tracker still lists the measure as Passed House — so the proposed remote-access authority has not become law. Unite.AI said the bill would amend the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to cover remote access by foreign persons to items under US jurisdiction.

The allegations behind the scrutiny

Reuters reported that Huang said on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The New York Times reported that the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed, and that US authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Jensen and Alice Huang are not related, Reuters said. Reuters could not independently verify that allegation, which China has denied. That allegation is reported here as an allegation, not as an established finding.

Megaspeed has faced scrutiny from US authorities over suspicions it helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips that were subject to US export controls, Reuters reported. The company has denied illegally diverting chips to China. In a statement on Thursday, Megaspeed said it had cooperated with inspections by the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, hired a US law firm to inventory its GPUs and verify compliance, welcomed scrutiny and was committed to complying with US export-control laws.

Reuters reported that Nvidia and the US Commerce Department did not respond to requests for comment. It said Alice Huang had business dealings and investment ties with several leading Chinese technology companies, including Tencent and Alibaba, according to two people familiar with the matter. Tencent said its computing procurement, leasing and operations complied with applicable laws and regulations, including export controls, and said it had no knowledge of, or involvement in, any alleged unlawful activities referenced in the reports. Alibaba did not respond to a request for comment, Reuters said.

Grey-market stockpiling and market reaction

Tougher enforcement prospects have also fuelled grey-market demand, with traders stockpiling restricted chips, two people told Reuters. Reuters reported Alibaba fell as much as 7.1% in Hong Kong on Thursday, while AI developers Z.AI and MiniMax both dropped at least 7% — reported moves on the day, not a forecast.

What to watch

Whether the Senate acts on RASA, and whether Commerce uses or seeks authority over remote access. Until either happens, Reuters describes precautionary moves by companies relying on a route US law has not yet closed.
